items.stem: On the plot, king minus man plus woman ends up closest to queen. What does this suggest about the word positions?

options.text: Man to king is the same step as woman to queen, so a relationship shows up as a direction.
options.feedback: Nobody names the relationship. It appears because words used in similar ways get similar positions.

options.text: The model stores a definition of queen as a female king and looks that definition up.
options.feedback: The model stores positions and holds no definitions. The match comes from distances.

options.text: The model checks a list of royal titles and picks the one that fits the sum.
options.feedback: There is no list. Positions are learned from text, and in this demo they were placed by hand.

options.text: Queen was the only word left on the plot after all the others were removed.
options.feedback: Many words remain on the plot. The result circle is nearest to queen.

items.stem: A vendor says its hiring tool is "only 3 percent biased" based on a word-analogy test. What is a reasonable response?

options.text: Ask how it was measured, since analogy tests can produce part of the result.
options.feedback: Embeddings reflect their corpus, and the analogy method adds to the result. A single tidy number needs an explanation.

options.text: Accept the number, because it comes from a mathematical test of the model.
options.feedback: A calculation can measure the wrong thing. The method needs checking too.

options.text: Add an instruction to the prompt telling the model to ignore gender in its answers.
options.feedback: A prompt cannot remove the pattern, because it is built into the positions the model uses.

options.text: Conclude that the model has no bias, because a program has no opinions of its own.
options.feedback: Bias here comes from patterns in the text the model was built from, and it needs no opinions.

items.stem: The sentences "How do I sign up for a class?" and "How do I drop a class?" share five words. In the demo, what is their similarity score?

options.text: Low, because the two sentences mean opposite things.
options.feedback: The two arrows point in very different directions, so the score is low even though many words match.

options.text: High, because the two sentences share five words with each other.
options.feedback: Counting shared words is what a keyword search does. The score compares meaning.

options.text: Exactly 1, because the two sentences are almost the same length.
options.feedback: Length has no effect. The score compares direction only.

options.text: Exactly 0, because the two sentences are different sentences.
options.feedback: The score drops to 0 only when the arrows are at right angles. These two are about 72 degrees apart.

items.stem: A student asks how to avoid being charged twice for an enrollment. The best help page is titled "Idempotency keys". Why might a search by meaning still find it?

options.text: The question and the page sit at similar positions, though they share no words.
options.feedback: This is retrieval: finding the text whose position is nearest to the question.

options.text: The search matches any page that contains the word charged.
options.feedback: That is keyword search. It would miss a page that lacks the word.

options.text: The search reads every page in full each time to find the answer.
options.feedback: Retrieval compares positions, which is much cheaper than reading every page.

options.text: The page title is rewritten automatically to match the question.
options.feedback: Nothing is rewritten. The two texts are compared by position.
